framework: European Commission, Cloud Sovereignty Framework v1.2.1 (Oct 2025)
rule: SEAL view (PLAN S7b, D12, D15, D16). SEAL rates a provider's service per sovereignty objective; this view states the minimum SEAL a provider service should reach, per objective, for each kind of data to meet its LTM level (DESIGN.md 3.4: LTM mapping, not the Commission's). It never rates the client or any provider. SOV-1, SOV-7 and SOV-8 are not mapped: they are provider-selection criteria in the placement matrix (S7). For zones outside the EU, read 'EU' as 'the allowed zone' (LTM generalisation).
intro: When the European Commission buys cloud services, it rates each provider's service from SEAL-0 to SEAL-4 on eight sovereignty objectives, such as legal, data, operational and supply chain. SEAL rates a provider's service, not your organisation. Sovereign IQ uses SEAL to show what level of provider service each kind of your data needs.
l4Note: The L4 row asks for SEAL-4 on several objectives. The Commission's implementation guidance (1 Jun 2026) says SEAL-4 is not relevant today, given the dependence on chips and hardware; LTM will revisit the row when the updated framework is published (D22).

tenderResults.statement: Commission sovereign cloud tender, as reported by the Commission on 17 Apr 2026: eligibility minimum SEAL-2; the Post Telecom-led partnership (with OVHcloud and CleverCloud), STACKIT and Scaleway reached SEAL-3; the Proximus-led partnership using S3NS reached SEAL-2. Results for the offers in that tender only; no per-objective levels or scores were published. Consultant view only (D20).

levels.name: No sovereignty
levels.wording: Service, technology or operations under exclusive control of non-EU third parties, governed entirely in non-EU jurisdictions
levels.plain: The service is controlled and governed entirely outside the EU.

levels.name: Jurisdictional sovereignty
levels.wording: EU law formally applies with limited practical enforceability; exclusive control of non-EU third parties
levels.plain: EU law applies on paper, but control sits outside the EU and EU law is hard to enforce.

levels.name: Data sovereignty
levels.wording: EU law applicable and enforceable, with material non-EU dependencies; indirect control of non-EU third parties
levels.plain: EU law applies and can be enforced, but the service still depends materially on parties outside the EU.

levels.name: Digital resilience
levels.note: Later Commission documents (1 Jun 2026) call this level Technological Sovereignty or technological autonomy; v1.2.1 wording shown
levels.wording: EU law applicable and enforceable, EU actors exercising meaningful but not full influence
levels.plain: EU law applies and can be enforced, and EU actors have meaningful, though not full, influence over the service.

levels.name: Full digital sovereignty
levels.wording: Technology and operations under complete EU control, subject only to EU law, with no critical non-EU dependencies
levels.plain: The service is fully under EU control, subject only to EU law, with no critical dependence on parties outside the EU.
